This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh. Microsoft is apologizing for last week's
outlook outage. Charles Lamanna, the company's executive vice president of co-pilot agents and
platform, said in a social media statement this morning that Thursday's incident was caused by an
undetected software bug that overwhelmed servers when traffic surged. Recovery took longer than
usual because restarting servers triggered more failures. Senator Chris Van Hollen knows he is the
underdog in the fight to unseat Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader, but the Maryland Democrat
tells NPR he can muster the support he needs to win. Here's NPR's Eric McDaniel. By some measures,
Chuck Schumer is the most unpopular politician in America. Many voters don't like his party either.
Only some 40 percent hold a favorable view of Democrats, but they did just give the Senate
Minority Leader and his party huge governing majorities. And Senator Van Hollen actually
tells NPR that's part of a larger plea for something new. People around the country are
looking for change, and my colleagues are listening to people around the country.
Public pressure could move senators into Van Hollen's column, but picking the Senate Majority Leader
is a closed-door, closed-ballot election, and it's not until December 1st anything could happen.
Eric McDaniel, NPR News Washington. At least six people were injured after Ukraine
launched a large-scale drone attack on targets in Russia and the occupied territories overnight.
NPR's Charles Mains has more from Moscow. What appeared to mark the largest combined
drone counterattack by Kiev since Russia launched its full-scale invasion nearly five years ago,
Russia said its air defenses successfully intercepted the Ukrainian barrage,
a claim that stood at odds with reports of damage at several large Russian oil and industrial
facilities. Also hit, the lone bridge linking occupied Crimea to mainland Russia, a project
seen as a physical symbol of Russia's hold over the peninsula, it illegally annexed from Ukraine
back in 2014. The local Moscow-backed authorities reported a halt to traffic along the bridge.
The Kremlin later dismissed the damage as minor. Charles Mains, NPR News, Moscow.
Lindsay Clancy will face another trial for the deaths of her three children in 2023.
Massachusetts prosecutors asked a judge today to set a date for a jury trial.
Deborah Becker of Member Station WBUR was at the hearing in Plymouth. During the brief hearing,
prosecutors requested a date for a jury trial but did not directly commit to once again pursuing
first-degree murder charges. Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington expects the district attorney
will not seek lesser charges where a jury could be waived. When they say that the case is going
to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the D.A. that they intend to proceed on
first-degree murder indictments. Clancy's case ended in a mistrial two months ago. The next
trial is set to begin March 29th. For NPR News, I'm Deborah Becker in Boston. It's NPR.
Customers with some major banks are reporting problems accessing their online accounts today.
The website downdetector.com lists Bank of America, Chase, Wells Fargo, Truist,
as well as the Zell Money Transfer Service among those difficult for some people to access.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt has arrived in the Middle East where the U.S. has been engaged in
more than eight months of war with Iran. President Trump is expected to discuss Iran
during his nuclear talks with the leaders of Russia and China
during his visit to Asia for two major summits. Judy Heumann was fed up with being denied access
to basic parts of life as a wheelchair user. So in 1977, she helped lead a month-long sit-in
of a federal building to demand change. NPR's Janaki Mehta reports a new feature film tells
that story. The new movie Being Human is about how a band of activists made the government enforce
its first civil rights law for people with disabilities. Now, 50 years since that battle
was won, it's being fought again. And it is our job to carry on her legacy and keep that
fire burning all these decades later. That's 23-year-old disability rights activist Kaylee
Brendel who runs an organization called Judy's League. She started it to push back against the
Trump administration's efforts to roll back the very protections Judy Heumann helped win. She says
watching the film gave her new resolve and reminded her this battle had been won once before.
That's Janaki Mehta. It's NPR.
